meta.title: Policy Window Monitor — Chile
meta.headline: 4 policy windows are open in Chile: 1 opened by a problem, 3 by politics. The fuel-price window is likely to close this week with a law; approval fell to new lows.
meta.topicsHeadline: Three windows have no evidence-based alternative in circulation yet, including the new one on fuel prices.
meta.note: Pilot run. The latest week's levels are proposed and await review. A flagged window is a likely opening, not a certainty, and not an endorsement of any proposal.

topics.name: Organised crime & Rules on the Use of Force (RUF)
topics.problem: Crime is the top problem in polls (CEP 57%), with sustained attention.
topics.politics: Level 3 in W5, then 2 after the decision: the mixed-committee report was approved on 7 Oct (Cámara 111–23–5, Senate 29–15–1).
topics.policy: Eight graduated rules, from police presence to lethal force. A bill from the previous government, adopted by this one.
topics.frames: 'Security as a precondition' vs proportionality and human rights. Partially converging.
topics.changed: Problem proposed 3→2: government figures show homicides −18% and violent robberies −19%; one nightclub shooting (16 Nov). Topic stays closed.
topics.reopen: Implementation controversy or a use-of-force incident

topics.name: Calles sin Violencia replaced by Plan FOCO
topics.problem: Level 2 in W4–W5, then 1 as attention faded. Problem broker: Carolina Tohá, who calls the programme central to reversing the rise in homicides.
topics.politics: The 2027 budget replaces Calles sin Violencia with FOCO. Barrio Prioritario is cut 43.4%; the crime-prevention undersecretariat gets +2.9%.
topics.policy: Two named alternatives compete. Undersecretary Pilar Giannini says FOCO has a stronger design and measurement; no evaluation of either is published.
topics.changed: Under the v0.4 rule this is no longer a window: the problem stream has been weak since W6, so the budget decision on Plan FOCO is moving on politics alone. The Cámara voted the Security budget on 10–12 Nov; results not yet coded.
topics.reopen: A rise in homicides, or an evaluation of either plan

topics.name: Migration: expulsions and detention
topics.problem: Immigration concern fell to 13% (CEP). 1,468 expulsions since March (secondary source).
topics.politics: Law dispatched on 20 Oct (Senate 37–0–1): home entry with a judicial order, re-entry ban raised from 3 to 5 years. Deputies rejected 60-day detention; the President publicly challenged them.
topics.policy: Bill adopted. A separate bill to criminalise irregular entry is pending (stage not verified).
topics.frames: Control and enforcement vs rights. Not assessed in detail.
topics.changed: No new activity.
topics.reopen: Detention reform or irregular-entry offence revived

topics.name: Administrative sentence reductions ('caso Rabat')
topics.timing: Rabat notified 17 Nov; defence due within 10 working days (he may file early); floor vote expected about 30 Nov–early Dec
topics.problem: Focusing event: 56 reductions for sexual offences against minors, plus reductions for crimes against humanity and for 115 foreign nationals convicted of drug offences. Cadem (27 Oct): 94% reject the reductions; 77% disapprove of the minister's handling.
topics.politics: Accusation (three chapters) filed 12 Nov; committee constituted 17 Nov with a 3–2 opposition majority. Count: 75 for, 76 against, 4 undecided; 78 needed. The PDG gives its deputies freedom; some UDI-bench deputies waver; Kast backs Rabat. 79% disagree with keeping him (Criteria, 15 Nov).
topics.policy: The minister advocates a named fix and has access to decision venues. No bill filed.
topics.frames: 'Illegitimate error' vs 'legal compliance'. Partially converging against the reductions.
topics.changed: Committee constituted (chair Raúl Soto, PPD) and Rabat notified on 17 Nov. The count is on a knife-edge: 75 for, 76 against, 4 undecided (El Mercurio, 17 Nov). The PDG dropped a bloc vote after the spokesperson called it 'un cúmulo de deseos'; five UDI-bench deputies are wavering. Politics stays at 2, as the reviewer set.

topics.name: Pension funds D and E losses
topics.problem: The Superintendent told the Cámara Labour committee (26 Oct) derivative losses were about US$10.1bn at 30 Sep, easing to about US$7bn by 20 Oct. Fund E −7.56% and Fund D −4.73% year to date. Attention fading after October's rebound.
topics.politics: Sanction process against 7 AFPs opened (20 Oct) and a committee session held. No executive bill.
topics.policy: Compensation and duration limits are mentioned, but no actor meets the entrepreneur definition.
topics.frames: Excessive portfolio duration (regulator) vs systemic failure of individual capitalisation. Not converging.
topics.changed: No coverage for a second week; window closed for attention faded.
topics.closing: Attention faded as Fund E recovered
topics.reopen: New losses, sanction results, or the compensation bill moving

topics.name: Employment recovery
topics.problem: Unemployment 9.8% (Jul–Sep, INE), highest since 2021; over 1 million unemployed; women 10.5%. Manufacturing jobs −8.1%. Cadem: job-instability worry 71%.
topics.politics: The executive frames Sala Cuna as an employment measure. The SENCE training budget was rejected in the mixed committee.
topics.policy: No dedicated job-creation bill.
topics.changed: Problem held at 2: Q3 household consumption slowed to 0.7%. Politics at the reviewed 1; window closing. INE unemployment (Aug–Oct) on 27 Nov.
topics.closing: Attention fading; no government step on employment
topics.reopen: INE unemployment on 27 Nov, Q3 GDP on 18 Nov, or an employment measure

topics.name: Sala Cuna Universal (Boletín 14.782-13)
topics.problem: The minister frames female unemployment above 10% and the 20-female-worker threshold (Art. 203) as a hiring barrier.
topics.politics: Chamber approval on 18 Nov (132–0–12; financing 114–1–29). Financing: 0.30% employer contribution offset by lower unemployment-insurance contributions. Senate third reading next.
topics.policy: Bill with a co-payment subsidy (50% for the most vulnerable 40%, 30% for the 41–60% band; regional source).
topics.frames: Employment for women vs 'negocio' (opposition criticism of the co-payment).
topics.changed: The Chamber approved Sala Cuna Universal 132–0 (12 abstentions) and its financing 114–1–29 on 18 Nov; Rau promised a 20% co-payment cap in a later bill. Senate third reading 24–25 Nov.

topics.name: Budget 2027 and fiscal consolidation
topics.timing: Chamber third reading 23 Nov; mixed committee; deadline 29 Nov
topics.problem: The Chamber dispatched Budget 2027 early on 13 Nov with seven ministry lines (six on the Chamber floor in votes on 10–13 Nov: Education, Interior, Segegob, Mining, Women, Culture; Science had already lost its funds in the mixed committee) and without the authorisation to borrow up to US$25bn, a defeat for the government.
topics.politics: Senate 17–19 Nov: most lines approved, debt authorisation restored 31–10 after a cross-party deal; Hacienda protocols on health (CLP 28bn for Ricarte Soto) and education (CLP 35bn for Yo Elijo Mi PC). Third reading in the Chamber on 23 Nov; deadline 29 Nov.
topics.policy: Government austerity path (structural balance −1.8% of GDP); restoration amendments; CFA calls for a fiscal-sustainability agreement.
topics.frames: Fiscal responsibility vs protection of social spending. Not converging.
topics.changed: The Senate restored the borrowing (up to about US$25bn; US$25.6bn per Radio UChile) authorisation 31–10 (PC, DC and PPD on board in exchange for US$160m for the FAPP and health and education protocols) and approved most lines on 17–19 Nov; municipal security funds go to a mixed committee. 'Caso Firmas': two senators' travel permits were withdrawn during the vote; the prosecutor opened an inquiry. Politics proposed 2→3. (The Senate dispatched the bill at 02:17 on 20 Nov with Agriculture rejected 14–14: W11.)

topics.name: Health budget: Ricarte Soto, immunisation, primary care
topics.problem: Senator Juan Luis Castro and health unions oppose the $28,000m Ricarte Soto cut and cuts to vaccines, primary care, mental health, dental and palliative care.
topics.politics: An executive amendment supplemented Ricarte Soto. Health passed 13–11 in the mixed committee; the primary-care programme was rejected.
topics.policy: Restore Ricarte Soto (partly done); raise primary-care per-capita funding without merging programmes; protect immunisation and mental health.
topics.frames: Efficiency vs protection of guaranteed coverage. Not converging.
topics.changed: The Senate approved the Health line 38–1 after Hacienda added CLP 28bn for Ricarte Soto (18 Nov). Window closed: decision taken. The 21–21 vote on gender-affirming care is tracked as T25.
topics.closing: Decision taken: both chambers approved the Health line with Ricarte Soto restored (Senate 38–1, 18 Nov)
topics.reopen: A cut in the mixed committee or in implementation

topics.name: Fuel prices
topics.timing: Law in force; cap until 7 Apr 2027
topics.problem: A national truckers' strike (9–12 Nov), joined by intercity buses and No+TAG, blocked highways over diesel prices after six consecutive rises. On 15 Nov, 97% had heard of it and about 80% backed it (Cadem, Criteria); 86% found it justified.
topics.politics: Ley 21.857 (published 17 Nov) caps petrol at its 5 Nov price and diesel at that price minus $100 until 7 Apr 2027, widens the truckers' diesel-tax refund (90/65/50% by size) and doubles the buses' toll refund to 70%. Passed 125–3 and 33 in favour; cost CLP 820,587m (Dipres). Quiroz promised working groups for fishers and extreme zones.
topics.policy: Executive bill to change Mepco; Hacienda considering fiscal savings to moderate rises. Bonuses for taxi drivers, school transport and artisanal fishers were extended in September.
topics.frames: 'Social urgency' (President) vs 'fuel is still cheap for the region' (Minister Mas).
topics.changed: Window closed with a decision, as the reviewer anticipated on 18 Nov: Ley 21.857 passed the Chamber 125–3 and the Senate 33 in favour on 16 Nov, was published on 17 Nov, and diesel fell $141.9 and petrol $38.7 from 19 Nov. Cost US$820m (Dipres). Critics on left and right call it a reward for blockades and a double standard (Briones, Vodanovic, Huenchumilla, Peña, Tironi).
topics.closing: Decision taken: Ley 21.857 passed on 16 Nov and published on 17 Nov; prices fell on 19 Nov
topics.reopen: Prices rising again before the cap expires on 7 Apr 2027, or a new strike

precedents.text: 32 truckers' strikes in 36 years, plus announced strikes. In 24 of the 29 with a known date, diesel prices had been rising beforehand.
2008: a strike over the diesel tax ended with the government agreeing to refund 80% of the specific tax that year and 100% from 2009.
2022: a week-long strike ended with an agreement on fuel-price stabilisation, transport rates and security.

topics.name: Economic slowdown and technical recession
topics.timing: Imacec October 1 Dec; monetary policy meeting 15 Dec
topics.problem: Q3 GDP −1.1% y/y and −1.8% q/q (Central Bank, 18 Nov); mining −14.7%, investment −6.7%, household consumption +0.7%. Jan–Sep −0.5%; economists expect a negative 2026. Q2 revised to 0.0%, so no two consecutive falls.
topics.politics: No growth plan or bill. The Economy Minister promised to 'redoblar esfuerzos' on investment projects; the PPD announced an interpellation of Quiroz. 60% expect the economy to worsen (Criteria, 15 Nov).
topics.changed: Q3 GDP fell 1.1% y/y and 1.8% q/q (18 Nov), investment −6.7%; problem proposed 2→3. The revision of Q2 to 0.0% means no 'technical recession' on the data. The PPD announced an interpellation of Quiroz; no growth plan, so politics stays 1.

topics.politics: No government response found (level 0).

topics.name: Science ministry: internal crisis and the science budget
topics.problem: The Science line of Budget 2027 was rejected in the mixed committee; the university rectors' council (CRUCh) puts the 2027 budget at a 10% real cut on 2026, putting Fondequip, Fondef, FIU, InES and graduate scholarships at risk (El Mercurio, 2 Nov). The Academy of Sciences warns lost capacity could take decades to recover. Coverage this week is about the internal conflict, not the cuts.
topics.politics: Conflict between Minister Lincolao and Undersecretary Rossi ended with Rossi's resignation (19 Nov) after Interior Minister Alvarado backed the minister; Kast called it a minor dispute. Hacienda rejected the minister's AI tax incentive. The OpenAI memorandum (16 Nov) was taken to the Comptroller.
topics.frames: Mismanagement and a divided team (government and press) vs. a budget cut that harms science (scientific community, CRUCh). Not converging.
topics.changed: Undersecretary Rossi resigned (accepted 19 Nov; Carolina Calvo acting) and Minister Lincolao stays with Interior's backing: a change of people that settles the conflict rather than opening a new agenda. Lincolao's OpenAI memorandum went to the Comptroller. The Senate restored the Science line after midnight on 20 Nov (W11).

method.framework: The monitor applies a modified version of Kingdon's Multiple Streams Framework, adapted with Zahariadis and, for Latin America's presidential systems, Sanjurjo (2020). Every week it reads a bounded list of sources for each country, rates the problem and politics streams for each topic, and flags a potential policy window when both show a signal. The policy stream (ideas, entrepreneurs, bills and their evidence) is analysed separately once a window is flagged.
process: Collect and transcribe the week's material from the country's source list: headlines and descriptions for everything, full text or transcripts only for items on monitored topics and for the weekly political review programmes.

Analyse the material for common themes against the concepts of the problem stream (focusing events, indicator changes, feedback, salience, frame consensus) and the politics stream (government approval, government intentions and agenda tools, national mood, organised forces, events within government). Each coded item keeps its context: source, programme, speaker and date.
Read each signal against the topic's precedents (past episodes such as strikes, protests or earlier windows on the same issue) and its own baseline of attention.
Weigh each concept by corroboration: it gains strength when it appears in more than one independent source in the same week.
Propose a level for each stream and topic, with a short rationale citing the items behind it.
A reviewer reads the proposed signals and their rationales and approves, changes or rejects them.

publicLimitations: Windows are hard to anticipate; the monitor estimates likely windows and can be wrong.
Levels rest on reviewer judgement. Explicit level descriptions, quotes with context and corroboration reduce, but do not remove, subjectivity.
A bounded source list can miss what happens outside it; a discovery net for coverage spikes and reviewers' additions partly correct this.
Some sources are behind paywalls or only available as audio or video.
Media attention favours dramatic topics over technical ones; polls and indicators partly balance this.
A flagged window is a likely opening, not a certainty, and not an endorsement of any proposal.

rules: A potential window is flagged when the problem and politics streams are both at level 2 or 3 in the same week.
Whichever stream reached level 2 first sets the coupling: problem window (consequential) or political window (doctrinal).
The politics level is lowered by one when approval or national mood is clearly against the move, or when coalition arithmetic suggests blocking.
Executive signals take precedence over congressional ones.
A level carries forward up to two weeks without new items, then drops one level.
The policy stream is checked only for topics where a window has been flagged.

From W10 each stream level rests on concept checks: one check per topic and concept (for example, fuel prices as a focusing event, and separately as a salient issue), each with its own rationale, evidence and strength (1 a mention or single source; 2 substantive, from two or more independent sources or one first-hand source; 3 decisive). The reviewer approves the concept checks first and the stream level second.

Budget topics count in the problem stream only when there is an event: a cut that draws coverage, a line rejected or not approved, a failed vote or a deadlock. Routine budget debate is technical and is coded in the politics stream (from W10, reviewer's rule).

Why frame consensus: Matthei, from the governing side's sector, called the handling of the case absurd, so criticism is no longer only from the opposition. One source this week. (UDI's president also called the decrees 'a serious political error', coded under politics.)

Why coalition or vote: the accusation was filed (12 Nov) and its review committee drawn with a 3–2 opposition majority (16 Nov), which is a formal step. But the opposition has about 65 of the 78 votes, the PDG swing bloc (14) will not commit, and UDI and the governing coalition expect to reject it. Strength 2: step taken, outcome open. Update (20 Nov): the vote is on a knife-edge: El Mercurio's count (17 Nov) is 75 for, 76 against and 4 undecided; Pauta puts the opposition at 62 plus 12 PDG, four short of 78. The PDG dropped a bloc vote after the spokesperson's 'cúmulo de deseos' remark, and five deputies on the UDI bench are wavering, which answers the reviewer's point that support inside the governing coalition is not settled. Rabat was notified on 17 Nov; the floor vote is expected around 30 Nov to early December. Strength stays 2: outcome open.

Why government intention: from Vietnam the President took responsibility and confirmed full support for Rabat. The executive intends to resist, not act; since executive signals take precedence, this holds the stream at 2. Update (20 Nov): Rabat says he will defeat the accusation and may file his defence early; Kast, at APEC, questioned the accusation and the threats against Quiroz. Strength unchanged.

Why indicator change: the Central Bank's job-ads index fell for a twelfth month (W9, one source). No new labour indicator this week; INE publishes on 27 Nov. The stream level of 2 is carried from the reviewed W9. Update (20 Nov): Q3 national accounts show household consumption slowing to 0.7% (2.5% in Q1), read as a sign of weak labour income. A second indicator alongside the job-ads index, from an official release. Strength proposed 1→2; the reviewer decided 1 on the partial week, so this check needs a new decision.
Why salience: one talk-show episode on unemployment as the top concern (W9). As the reviewer noted, coverage this week is thin.

Why national mood: 53% expect job prospects to worsen (Criteria, 15 Nov), in two outlets. Mood only: no government move on employment this week, so by the same rule used for Growth & recession the stream level is 1.

Why a focusing event: the Chamber sent the budget to the Senate with seven ministry lines (six on the Chamber floor in votes on 10–13 Nov: Education, Interior, Segegob, Mining, Women, Culture; Science had already lost its funds in the mixed committee) and without the authorisation to borrow up to US$25bn, which the press called a defeat for the government. Under the budget rule a rejection is the kind of event that makes the budget a problem. Caution from the second check: rejecting lines in the Chamber and restoring them in the Senate is a fairly common budget cycle, and there is no sign of public attention. Update (20 Nov): no new rejection that drew coverage in 13–19 Nov: the Senate's rejection of municipal security funds (19 Nov) had little coverage, and the Agriculture line's 14–14 rejection came after midnight on 20 Nov, so it belongs to W11. Strength unchanged.

Why government intention: the Finance Minister promised to restore the rejected lines in the Senate and keeps the consolidation target while paying about US$700m for the truckers' deal. Three outlets. It is a promise: no funds have been restored yet, so it is not coded as use of the budget tool.

Why coalition or vote: the Chamber result shows the government lacks a majority for its budget as drafted. This arithmetic is the reason the stream is held at 2 instead of 3. Update (20 Nov): the Senate approved most lines on 17–19 Nov and restored the borrowing (up to about US$25bn; US$25.6bn per Radio UChile) authorisation 31–10 after a deal that brought PC, DC and PPD senators on board (US$160m for the pension reform's FAPP fund and health commitments). Municipal security funds were rejected and go to a mixed committee. The 'Caso Firmas' (travel permits of two senators withdrawn, allegedly to change the quorum; the prosecutor opened an inquiry) shows how tight the arithmetic is. The restoration vote is decisive, so the check rises. Strength proposed 2→3; the reviewer decided 2 on the partial week, so this check needs a new decision.

Why coalition or vote: the Chamber approved the Health budget 82–41, restored primary-care funds and raised Ricarte Soto funding. A decision in one chamber; the Senate remains. No problem-stream item this week. Update (20 Nov): Hacienda's health protocol (13 amendments) restored about CLP 28bn for Ricarte Soto and kept primary-care programmes; the opposition still disputes the per-capita rise. Strength unchanged.

Why a focusing event: the amendment to restore the Education budget failed 72–72 on 11 Nov, so Education stays rejected. One event (W9), reported by two outlets; the 16 Nov item is a recap, not a second rejection. A failed vote is an event under the budget rule. No measure of public attention yet.

Why organised forces: the teachers' union called a national march and work stoppage for 24 Nov over the education budget. One outlet, reporting the union's own call. Update (20 Nov): the teachers' union ratified the 24 Nov strike on 17 Nov and confirmed the route on 19 Nov; the CUT–Confech march of 18 Nov against the budget cuts drew protests at 24 points. Several independent sources, but the main strike is still ahead, so strength stays 2.

Why government intention: the truckers' deal doubles the toll refund for intercity buses, from 35% to 70% (W9 item coded under fuel prices). A commitment inside a signed deal. Audit (20 Nov): D158 is coded under T21 and is no longer cited here; the check now rests on Ley 21.857's toll provisions (D311), coded under T16.

Why organised forces: No+TAG joined the blockades demanding lower tolls, a flat tariff and forgiveness of TAG debts, and said it had no agreement with the government (W9). Update (20 Nov): No+TAG, which did not sign the deal, ended its road protests on 13 Nov. The toll refund for buses rose from 35% to 70% in Ley 21.857 (coded under T21). Strength unchanged.
Why national mood: 64% support the higher toll refund (Cadem). One poll question, one outlet.

Why indicator change: the Central Bank's expectations survey cut 2026 growth to 0% (10 Nov). A primary source; Q3 GDP on 18 Nov will confirm or ease it. Update (20 Nov): the Central Bank's Q3 national accounts (18 Nov): GDP −1.1% y/y and −1.8% q/q, investment −6.7%. One release, reported by several outlets and counted once. It is decisive for attention to growth. It does not confirm a 'technical recession': Q2 was revised from −0.2% to 0.0% y/y and +0.1% q/q, so there are not two consecutive falls. Strength proposed 2→3; the reviewer decided 2 on the partial week, so this check needs a new decision.

Why frame consensus: the Finance Minister himself said the economy is 'technically' in recession, adopting the critics' description. One actor, so strength 1; it becomes consensus if the opposition and business describe it the same way. Update (20 Nov): economists at XTB, SURA, Itaú and Principal now expect 2026 to close negative (Jan–Sep −0.5%); the government (Economy Minister Mas, Undersecretary Vallebona) also calls the figure bad. Government and analysts describe the problem the same way. Strength proposed 1→2; the reviewer decided 1 on the partial week, so this check needs a new decision.
Why indicator change: the Children's Ombudsman reports more than 41,000 children waiting for protection places. One source (CIPER, citing Emol).
Why feedback: Matthei called the government's security plan 'pure bluff', a judgement on how an existing plan performs. One voice, no data.

Why coalition or vote: regional budget lines passed the Chamber without rejection, credited to the earlier agreement with governors. Confirms a decision already taken. Update (20 Nov): the Senate approved the regional governments' line on 18 Nov. Strength unchanged.

Why government approval: Criteria 18% (−6), Cadem 27% (−2), both the lowest of the term, reported by seven outlets, with Panel Ciudadano near 20%. A decisive change that narrows room for unpopular moves.

Why national mood: 84% said the government should have acted sooner on fuel prices. The public is against the government's handling but in favour of the measures now on the table. Same two polls as the fuel-prices mood check, so not counted as new evidence. Update (20 Nov): Alfredo Joignant's closing segment on Tolerancia Cero (16 Nov) read the fall to 18% as a 40-point drop in under a year; Claudio Orrego (podcast Cómo te lo explico) said the government is 'playing with fire' by breaking promises. Commentary, not new measures; strength unchanged. Audit (20 Nov): D172 (the Cadem and Criteria strike polls) is coded under T21 and is no longer cited here; what remains is commentary, so strength proposed 2→1 (the reviewer decided 2 on the partial week).

Why events within government: criticism of La Moneda's advisers from inside the coalition, the President abroad until 22 Nov, and no cabinet change. Mentions only. Update (20 Nov): two remarks were replayed until they became the story: Agriculture Minister Campos on cheap fruit (Quiroz apologised for him on 16 Nov; he refused; a Libertario deputy asked for his removal) and the spokesperson's 'cúmulo de deseos' about the PDG (apology on 17 Nov, the PDG demanded a retraction). A UDI-bench deputy called some ministers 'un cero a la izquierda'; Kast ruled out a cabinet change. Several outlets, so the check rises. Strength proposed 1→2; the reviewer decided 1 on the partial week, so this check needs a new decision.

Why events within government: the minister and the undersecretary are in open conflict (dismissals on 13 Nov without the undersecretary's knowledge), the Interior Minister stepped in on 16 Nov and the spokesperson said on 17 Nov that the ministry 'has not worked as we expected' and the President 'will decide'. Four outlets; the spokesperson's statement is first-hand and decisive, because it puts a change of people on the table. Update (20 Nov): the conflict ended with a change of people: Undersecretary Carolina Rossi resigned (letter sent to Kast on 18 Nov, accepted effective 19 Nov; Carolina Calvo acting), hours after Interior Minister Alvarado publicly backed Minister Lincolao. Kast called the dispute minor. Several outlets; strength stays 3.

conceptSignals.rationale: Why government intention: the government dropped the minister's tax incentive from the AI bill after Hacienda objected, while the minister signs agreements with AI firms abroad. Two signals of what the executive intends on science and AI policy, pulling in different directions. Update (20 Nov): Lincolao defended the OpenAI memorandum she signed on 16 Nov as science diplomacy. Still no policy step on the science budget or the AI bill. Strength unchanged.

Why indicator change: ENAP's weekly estimate put diesel down $141.9 and petrol down $38.7 per litre from Thu 19 Nov, the first fall in almost four months. One official series reported by one outlet; it shows the problem easing, which supports a lower problem level from W11.

Why agenda tool (budget): Dipres's financial report costs the law at CLP 820,587m (about US$820m), financed from the Treasury and the sale of Treasury assets: funding added by law. One official source.

Why indicator change: the CNE's node-price review lowers regulated electricity bills by 4.4% on average for Jan–Jun 2027 in 13 of 16 regions (rises in Los Ríos, Los Lagos and Magallanes). An official measure easing the problem; one outlet. It argues against raising the problem level.

Why feedback: a Supreme Court order of about 17 Nov told the Justice ministry to decide a sentence-reduction request from a convicted child rapist 'a la brevedad'. It is evidence on how the reduction procedure works in practice. One outlet, but a first-hand court decision; strength 2.

Why agenda tool (budget): facing an opposition threat of a constitutional accusation, Quiroz put 2.2 million UTM (about US$160m) for the pension reform's FAPP fund explicitly into the 2027 budget. Funding added by the executive; one outlet (a second, T13, reports the same announcement and is not counted).

Why organised forces: public-sector unions opened pay talks on 16 Nov demanding 6.3% nominal (at least 2% real); Quiroz suspended one session because of the budget. One source; the pay round is a separate decision due later in the year.

Why agenda tool (budget): the Senate approved the Health line 38–1 after Hacienda added CLP 28bn for the Ricarte Soto Law, reversing the cut. Funding restored through the Budget Law in the second chamber, which settles the line: decisive. The 21–21 vote on gender-affirming care inside the same line is coded under T25.

Why agenda tool (budget): on 19 Nov Hacienda signed a cross-party protocol with the Senate's fourth mixed subcommittee: CLP 35bn back for Yo Elijo Mi PC (redesign promised for 2028) and extra higher-education funds. An executive funding decision that unblocks the line the Chamber rejected; decisive by itself. (The Senate approved Education 25–2 after midnight; that vote is W11.)

Why government intention: the Education protocol commits a working group with the rectors' council (CRUCh) in early 2027 on degree length, gratuidad fees and an income-contingent loan to replace the CAE. A written commitment, one source; it is a promise to study, not a bill, so the stream stays at 1.

Why coalition or vote: the Chamber's Finance committee approved the financing (17 Nov) and the floor approved the bill 132–0 with 12 abstentions and the financing 114–1–29 (18 Nov). The left objected to drawing on unemployment insurance but abstained rather than block. A decisive vote; the Senate's third reading is due 24–25 Nov.
Why government intention: Labour Minister Rau pledged a 20% cap on family co-payments in a later bill to secure votes. A commitment, one source.
Why salience: El Desconcierto framed the release as a deepening economic crisis. One outlet's emphasis; heavy and sustained coverage, or a poll ranking, would raise it.
Why government intention: the Economy Minister said the contraction 'nos exige redoblar esfuerzos' on unblocking investment projects. A statement with no plan, bill or measure: a mention.

Why coalition or vote: the PPD announced an interpellation of Quiroz over the economy and jobs (it needs a third of deputies), reported by two outlets. A parliamentary step by the opposition, not a vote on a measure; strength 2.

Why feedback: Deputy Araya asked the Comptroller whether the ministry could legally sign the OpenAI memorandum, and Senator Ibáñez sent formal requests. Oversight of a ministry decision; one outlet, strength 1.
Why focusing event: a shooting at a central Santiago nightclub (16 Nov) left one dead and seven injured. Sudden and violent, but one outlet and no follow-up coverage; strength 1.

Why indicator change: government figures show homicides down 18% and violent robberies down 19% year on year, and irregular northern-border entries down 85%. Official series (one source); they show the problem easing.

Why coalition or vote: the government's budget indication (filed 14 Nov) to bar public funding of cross-sex hormones and some surgeries for under-18s tied 21–21 twice in the Senate (18 Nov) and fell; Libertario deputies then threatened an accusation against Health Minister Chomalí. Two outlets; a failed vote is decisive for this week.
Why coalition or vote: the Partido Nacional Libertario openly mocked Kast's wreath at Ho Chi Minh's mausoleum, a rift inside the governing bloc. One outlet; a mention of strain, not a vote.

Why government intention: the Asia tour produced a strategic partnership with Vietnam and two agreements with China (17 Nov Xi bilateral). Foreign-policy commitments with no domestic topic attached; strength 1.

stories.title: The fuel law passed in a day, and the window closed
stories.text: Ley 21.857 passed the Chamber 125–3 and the Senate 33 in favour on 16 Nov and was published the next day; diesel fell $141.9 and petrol $38.7 from 19 Nov. With the decision taken the window is closed, while critics on left and right call the US$820m deal a reward for blockades.

stories.title: The Senate gives the budget back its borrowing
stories.text: The Senate restored the debt (about US$25bn) authorisation 31–10 after deals with PC, DC and PPD senators, and Hacienda signed protocols on health and education. The Chamber's third reading is on 23 Nov, with a mixed committee before the 29 Nov deadline.

stories.title: GDP fell 1.1% in the third quarter
stories.text: The Central Bank reported GDP down 1.1% year on year and 1.8% on the quarter, with investment down 6.7%. Revised data for the second quarter mean there is no 'technical recession', but economists now expect 2026 to close negative.

Focusing event.definition: A sudden, visible event (a crisis, disaster, scandal, strike, or a vote that fails) that draws attention to a problem at once.

Indicator change.definition: A movement in a regular measure (inflation, unemployment, crime, growth, waiting lists) that shows a problem getting worse or better.

Feedback.definition: Evidence on how an existing programme or decision works: evaluations, audits, implementation failures, complaints.

Salience.definition: How much the public attends to the issue: its rank among the 'most important problems' in polls, or sustained heavy coverage.

Frame consensus.definition: Actors on different sides describe the issue the same way and agree it is a problem.

Government approval.definition: Approval of the President or government in polls. Low approval narrows room for unpopular moves; high approval widens it.

National mood.definition: Broad public sentiment that pushes for or against action, such as support for a demand or economic pessimism.

Agenda tool used (urgency).definition: The executive puts a legislative urgency on a bill (simple, suma or discusión inmediata), forcing a timetable.

Agenda tool used (budget).definition: Funding is added, cut or restored through the Budget Law or by decree.

Government intention.definition: The executive announces a plan, files a bill or makes a commitment in a speech.

Coalition or vote.definition: Party positions, vote counts and votes in Congress that show whether a measure can pass.

Organised forces.definition: Unions, business groups, NGOs and other organised interests mobilising, striking or lobbying.

Events within government.definition: Cabinet changes, resignations or internal disputes that shift who decides.
